title: Why Jacaranda Health Spun Out the Maternity Hospital It Built
dek: Around 2017 a Kenyan maternal-health nonprofit decided it could not run its own hospital and serve government hospitals well at once, so it split in two.

story.event: Spinning out its own maternity hospital as a separate venture to concentrate on public hospitals
story.summary: Jacaranda Health, founded by Nick Pearson in Nairobi in 2011, began by running its own low-cost maternity hospitals. By about 2017, with its hospital struggling to break even and its work with government hospitals growing, the team judged that one organisation could not do both well; it spun the hospital out as a standalone social venture, Jacaranda Maternity, with its own chief executive and investors, while the nonprofit Jacaranda Health concentrated on public hospitals.
paragraphs: On 13 July 2011 a mobile antenatal clinic opened in Kariobangi, north-eastern Nairobi. It was the first service of Jacaranda Health, started by Nick Pearson after he left the Acumen Fund, where he had invested in Kenyan businesses; his wife, an obstetrician who had worked in western Kenya, helped inspire it. In August 2012 Jacaranda opened its first maternity hospital, in Ruiru, charging KSh7,900 for a delivery. In 2013 Pearson told an interviewer he wanted "to become the biggest chain of maternity hospitals in East Africa", with 25 hospitals in about five years.

A second hospital, in Kahawa West, opened in September 2014 with facilities for caesarean sections. In 2015 Jacaranda began working with two public hospitals outside Nairobi, and in January 2016 Pearson described the plan as keeping "a few of our own maternity centers of excellence" to drive innovation, then helping government copy good care in its hospitals. That mattered because, he later wrote, 80 per cent of Kenyan women still gave birth in government hospitals.

By 2017, Pearson wrote in a 2022 essay, the hospital was busy and well loved but "struggling to break even", while the nurse training and digital outreach built for its own wards were gaining ground in government facilities. He and his team judged that "doing both at once could be a recipe for excellence at neither": a hospital business and a government partner needed different leaders and different money. Advised by impact investors at the Tara Health Foundation, they kept both, separately. The hospital became a standalone social venture, Jacaranda Maternity, seeded with a loan and led by Sawan Shah, a new chief executive from financial services. The nonprofit kept the name Jacaranda Health; its own timeline dates its public-sector form to 2016 and its first prototypes, in three Kiambu County facilities, to 2017.

In 2018, by the nonprofit's account, its text-message service for mothers, PROMPTS, and its nurse-mentoring programme, MENTORS, formally launched in 50 hospitals; by 2024 it counted three million mothers reached and 23 partner counties. The hospital company, Pearson wrote, broke even by 2019 and raised investment from Johnson & Johnson Impact Ventures and others; in March 2026 it ran four hospitals around Nairobi. Pearson called the split "the single most important decision we made as a team".

quote.text: Ten dervishes can sleep on one rug, but two kings cannot be accommodated in a whole kingdom.
quote.locator: Chapter I (Of the Customs of Kings), Story III
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi was writing about rival princes whose father had divided his lands. Jacaranda's founders were not rivals, but they reached a similar conclusion: a hospital business and a government partner each needed its own head and its own money, and one organisation could not comfortably hold both.

reflection: What strikes me is that Jacaranda did not decide its hospital had failed. It decided that the hospital and the government work needed different people, different money and a different pace, and that asking one team to carry both was the larger risk.

You probably carry more than one kind of work as well, and each asks for a different version of you: patient and exact in one place, quick and outward in another. It can help to stop treating the strain between them as a personal failing, and to ask whether one of them simply needs its own time, its own help or its own name.
invitation: Pick the two pieces of work that pull hardest against each other this week. Give one of them a fixed morning of its own, written in your calendar, and let the other wait outside it.

cross_checks.claim: Jacaranda began in July 2011 with a mobile clinic and opened its first maternity hospital in Ruiru in 2012
Before the split, Jacaranda was already working with government hospitals to replicate its methods
The hospital was separated from the nonprofit and runs as its own company, Jacaranda Maternity, while the nonprofit works in the public health system
Pearson worked at the Acumen Fund in Nairobi before founding Jacaranda, and his wife is an obstetrician who worked in western Kenya

research_notes: Date of the split: Pearson's 2022 essay places the crossroads in 2017 ('Five years later, in 2017'), while Jacaranda's 2024 annual report dates the nonprofit's public-sector form to 2016, prototypes in three Kiambu facilities to 2017 and the formal launch of PROMPTS and MENTORS to 2018 (the slate's year). The story gives both and sets approx_date to 2017. Public-hospital start: the 2016 Blum Center piece says the first partnership was with two public hospitals in 2015; Jacaranda's own report starts its timeline with three Kiambu facilities in 2017. Both are given. Hospital outcomes: Pearson's April 2022 essay said Jacaranda Maternity had two busy hospitals, was opening a third and planned a Series B for ten more; Business Daily (March 2026) reports four facilities and an expansion target of six. The story uses the 2026 count and does not repeat the ten-hospital plan. The 2022 essay is first-person by Pearson but was published as sponsored content paid for by Johnson & Johnson Impact Ventures, an investor in Jacaranda Maternity; claims that rest on it alone (break-even by 2019, the Series A, the 'most important decision') are attributed to Pearson. The 80 per cent figure for births in government hospitals is Pearson's and is attributed. The nonprofit's 2024 report PDF uses a font whose embedded text extracts as a letter-substitution cipher in places; the timeline entries were read by decoding that substitution and agree with the readable portions. A 2016 CV of Pearson hosted by Duke University gives similar figures (two midwife-led hospitals; quality-improvement pilots in two public hospitals in 2015) but is not cited because it carries personal contact details. funding is 'mixed' because the nonprofit was grant-funded with patient fees and the spun-out hospital later took impact investment. The company field is given as 'Jacaranda' rather than 'Jacaranda Health' because the repeat screen matched the shared word 'Health' with an unrelated company (Helium Health, Nigeria); the organisation is the same Jacaranda Health throughout. Saadi's line comes from a tale of a king who divided his domains among quarrelling sons; it is applied by analogy, and the connection says the founders were not rivals.
